hints: Recall the link between power, work done or energy transferred, and time taken for that transfer.
teacher_walkthrough: Power is defined as the rate of doing work: $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ where $W$ is work done and $t$ is time taken.
Equivalently, power is the rate of energy transfer: $$P = \frac{E}{t}$$ where $E$ is energy transferred in time $t$.
The key phrase for the definition is work done per unit time or energy transferred per unit time.
walkthrough: B1: work done per unit time or energy transferred per unit time.
common_pitfalls: Stating $P = Fv$ or $P = VI$ without giving the defining statement of work done per unit time.
Confusing power with energy or work by omitting reference to time, e.g. saying power is work done.

hints: Start from $\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$, expand $\mathrm{J}$ to $\mathrm{N\,m}$, then expand $\mathrm{N}$ to SI base units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.
teacher_walkthrough: Power is work divided by time: $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ so the SI unit of power is $$\text{unit of } P = \frac{\text{unit of } W}{\text{unit of } t} = \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$$
Work is force times distance, so $$1\,\mathrm{J} = 1\,\mathrm{N} \times 1\,\mathrm{m}$$ giving $$\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}} = \mathrm{N\,m\,s^{-1}}$$
Force is mass times acceleration from $F = ma$, so $$1\,\mathrm{N} = 1\,\mathrm{kg} \times 1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} = \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$$
common_pitfalls: Leaving the answer in derived units such as $\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$ or $\mathrm{N\,m\,s^{-1}}$ instead of fully expanding to base units.
Incorrectly expanding the newton, e.g. using $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ and obtaining a wrong power of $\mathrm{s}$.

hints: Recall the physical meaning of intensity as power per unit area normal to the wave, so first find the SI base units of $I$ from part (a)(ii).
Rearrange the given equation to make $k$ the subject and write each quantity in SI base units: $f$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $A$ in $\mathrm{m}$, $v$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Combine the denominator $f^2 A^2 v$ into a single $\mathrm{m}$ and $\mathrm{s}$ power, then divide the intensity units by this and simplify the indices.
teacher_walkthrough: Intensity is power per unit area: $$I = \frac{P}{A}$$
From (a)(ii), unit of $P$ is $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}$ and unit of area $A$ is $\mathrm{m^2}$, so $$\text{unit of } I = \frac{\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}}{\mathrm{m^2}} = \mathrm{kg\,s^{-3}}$$

Rearrange $I = f^2 A^2 v k$ for $k$: $$k = \frac{I}{f^2 A^2 v}$$ so in units $$\text{unit of } k = \frac{\mathrm{kg\,s^{-3}}}{(\text{unit of } f)^2 \times (\text{unit of } A)^2 \times (\text{unit of } v)}$$

Frequency $f$ has unit $\mathrm{Hz} = \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, amplitude $A$ is a length with unit $\mathrm{m}$, speed $v$ has unit $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $$(\text{unit of } f)^2 = (\mathrm{s^{-1}})^2 = \mathrm{s^{-2}}$$ $$(\text{unit of } A)^2 = (\mathrm{m})^2 = \mathrm{m^2}$$
walkthrough: C1: intensity = power / area so units of $I$ are $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-3}}$.
C1: $k = I/(f^2 A^2 v)$ so units of $k$ are $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-3}/(s^{-2} \times m^2 \times m\,s^{-1})}$.
A1: SI base units of $k$ are $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
common_pitfalls: Using $\mathrm{Hz}$ or $\mathrm{s}$ for frequency instead of $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, giving $\mathrm{s^{2}}$ in the denominator instead of $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$.
Treating amplitude $A$ as dimensionless or forgetting to square both $f$ and $A$, which changes the powers of $\mathrm{m}$ and $\mathrm{s}$.
Leaving derived units in the final answer such as $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,Hz^{-2}\,m^{-3}\,s}$ instead of simplifying fully to SI base units.
